paragraphs.heading: Mountains on the seafloor
paragraphs.text: A mid-ocean ridge is a mountain system on the seafloor, built by plate tectonics. It marks a divergent plate boundary, where seafloor spreading widens an ocean basin. A ridge typically lies about 2,600 meters deep and rises some 2,000 meters above the deepest part of its basin. The first one found was the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, which splits the North and South Atlantic basins, and its position gave these ridges their name, even though most spreading centers are not in the middle of their oceans.

paragraphs.heading: One chain around the world
paragraphs.text: Ridges across the globe are linked by plate boundaries, and their path over the ocean floor looks like the seam of a baseball. Most of them join into one global system, the Ocean Ridge, which runs through every ocean. Its continuous mountain range is 65,000 km long, several times longer than the Andes, and the whole ridge system adds up to 80,000 km.

paragraphs.heading: How new crust is made
paragraphs.text: As the plates pull apart, mantle rock wells up beneath them, producing new seafloor and new oceanic lithosphere, the crust plus the colder, denser part of the mantle that together form the plates. The melt rises as magma through the weak line between the plates, erupts as lava and cools into new crust. It melts by decompression, as rising solid mantle passes its solidus temperature. The magma crystallizes into a basalt called MORB, with gabbro below it in the lower crust, and hydrothermal vents fed by this heat are common along the ridges.

paragraphs.heading: Older seafloor sits deeper
paragraphs.text: The rocks are youngest along the ridge axis and get older the farther you go from it. Depth follows age: a good rule is that seafloor depth is proportional to the square root of its age. Near the axis, hot, low-density mantle props up the crust. Farther away the plate cools, its mantle layer thickens and grows denser, and so older seafloor rests deeper.

paragraphs.heading: Magnetic stripes keep time
paragraphs.text: Spreading rates are worked out by mapping magnetic patterns in the crust on both sides of a ridge. When basalt erupted at the axis cools, iron-titanium oxides in it lock in the direction of Earth's magnetic field. Because the field has flipped at known times, the pattern of reversals dates the crust, and the age plus the distance from the axis gives the spreading rate. Rates run from about 10 to 200 mm a year.

paragraphs.heading: Slow ridges and fast ridges
paragraphs.text: Slow ridges, spreading under 40 mm a year like the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, have steep profiles, rift valleys up to 10–20 km wide and rugged crests with up to 1,000 m of relief. Fast ridges, over 90 mm a year like the East Pacific Rise, have gentle profiles and no rift valleys. The North Atlantic spreads at about 25 mm a year and the Pacific at 80–145 mm, and the highest known rate, over 200 mm a year, was on the East Pacific Rise in the Miocene. Ridges slower than 20 mm a year, such as the Gakkel Ridge in the Arctic, are called ultraslow.
